synopsis: D-optimal designs are useful when constraints make regular factorial test grids impossible, although they sacrifice orthogonality and can produce correlated estimates [f14105, f6803, f7224]. Under model assumptions, response-surface and D-optimal DOE establish local response models, curvature and optimum regions; the booklet recommends them for fine tuning thresholds and zones and exploring constrained physical design spaces [f7221, f7220]. After prototype arrival, modest DOE or D-optimal tests should estimate sensor, latency and braking residuals and initialise common parameters; the glossary places DOE in both the coverage and calibration streams [f7381, f14109]. This coverage role is limited: these methods cannot establish global corner-case coverage or operational probabilities and are poor for discontinuous behaviour [f7222, f7223]. An independent evidence base exists, but no off-road evidence is reported; statistics packages are typical tooling [f7226, f7225].

relations.note: Both identify constrained grids as a reason to use D-optimal designs.
Both recommend post-arrival DOE calibration of sensor, latency and braking residuals.
Suitability for constrained grids supports use in constrained physical design spaces.
Local response modelling and optimum estimation support threshold and zone fine tuning.
Correlated estimates add a specific limitation alongside sacrificed orthogonality.
Limits the glossary's coverage role: DOE cannot establish global coverage or operational probabilities.
Distinguishes local model capabilities from unavailable global coverage guarantees.
Discontinuous behaviour limits suitability for the recommended fine-tuning applications.
No reported off-road evidence qualifies the program's recommended use.
